title: Casts: Molds of the Nephron That Point to the Disease
summary: Explain how urinary casts form in the tubules, match each cast type to its kidney disease, recognize dysmorphic red cells and acanthocytes as glomerular bleeding, and tell cholesterol Maltese crosses from starch artifacts.

reviewer.note: Core lesson for Ch. 29: teaches Hit 1 (core: RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs), Hit 5 (waxy, broad, fatty and WBC casts) and Hit 17 (starch Maltese-cross artifact). Checked against Gaggar & Raju 2024 and Kubo 2025. Hit 1 says “glomerular disease, full stop”, but RBC casts occurred in 29% of biopsy-proven interstitial nephritis (register flag rv-rbc-casts); Hit 5 ties WBC casts to pyelonephritis and waxy casts to end-stage disease only (register flag rv-cast-specificity). Not taught: glitter cells (Hit 6), the > 30 WBC/hpf cut-off and “mucus is normal” (Hit 18) — not in the sources read.

objectives: Explain how casts form from uromodulin in the renal tubules and why a cast localizes disease to the kidney.
Match RBC, WBC, RTE, granular, waxy, fatty, bacterial and pigment casts to their usual conditions.
Recognize dysmorphic red cells and acanthocytes as markers of glomerular hematuria and know their limits.
Distinguish cholesterol Maltese crosses from starch artifacts under polarized light.

scenes.title: Blood in the urine — but from where?
scenes.altText: A urine cup tinted pink and a dipstick with a positive blood pad. A cartoon urinary tract: kidneys at the top, ureters, bladder. Question markers appear at the glomerulus, the tubules, the bladder. A token: “Same dipstick result — very different diseases.” The cartoon scientist holds a microscope slide.

cues.text: A patient’s urine has blood in it. The dipstick blood pad is positive.
But the blood could come from a damaged glomerulus, from the tubules, from a kidney stone or from the bladder. The dipstick cannot tell them apart.
The microscope can. What is trapped in the sediment points to where the trouble started.

scenes.title: A cast is a mold of the tubule
scenes.altText: A schematic tubule segment (a long channel). Uromodulin (Tamm–Horsfall protein) gel gathers inside the lumen, filling it into a cylinder; whatever is in the lumen at that moment — red cells, white cells, tubular cells, fat — is trapped in the gel. The cylinder slides out into the urine as a cast, shaped like the tubule. A hyaline cast (protein only) appears with a note: increases with strenuous exercise, dehydration and fever. A method token: read at least 10 fields at low (100×) and high (400×) power.

cues.text: Casts form inside the kidney tubules. The tubule cells secrete a protein called uromodulin, also known as Tamm–Horsfall protein.
In the tubule, this protein forms a gel that fills the channel and traps whatever is floating there: red cells, white cells, tubular cells or fat.
The gel plug then washes out into the urine as a cylinder shaped like the tubule. So any cast tells you the material came from the kidney itself.
A cast of protein alone is a hyaline cast. A few appear with strenuous exercise, dehydration or fever, without kidney disease.
To find casts, scan at least 10 fields at low power, 100 times, then confirm at high power, 400 times.

props.label: Any cast = material from the kidney

scenes.title: What is trapped tells you what is wrong
scenes.altText: A cast catalog fills in as cards. RBC casts → nephritic syndrome (glomerular bleeding); rarely interstitial nephritis. WBC casts → interstitial nephritis, nephritic syndrome or pyelonephritis. Renal tubular epithelial (RTE) and granular casts → acute tubular necrosis (RTE also interstitial nephritis). Waxy casts (broad, refractile, cracked edges) → renal failure, acute or chronic. Fatty casts and oval fat bodies → nephrotic-range proteinuria; cholesterol shows Maltese crosses under polarized light. Bacterial casts → bacterial pyelonephritis. Pigment casts → hemoglobin, myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis), bilirubin.

cues.text: Red-cell casts mean red cells were in the tubule, usually from a leaking glomerulus. They are the signature of nephritic syndrome, and rarely appear in interstitial nephritis.
White-cell casts point to inflammation in the kidney: interstitial nephritis, nephritic syndrome or pyelonephritis. Bacterial casts point to pyelonephritis.
Tubular epithelial cell casts and granular casts point to acute tubular necrosis, where tubule cells die and slough.
Waxy casts are broad, glassy and cracked. They form in slow, stagnant tubules, and are seen in renal failure, acute or chronic.
Fatty casts and oval fat bodies mean nephrotic-range protein loss. Under polarized light, their cholesterol shows Maltese crosses.

scenes.title: Dysmorphic red cells — and two Maltese crosses
scenes.altText: Two red-cell tokens: isomorphic (round, smooth central pallor) and dysmorphic (irregular, with blebs — the acanthocyte, a ring with protrusions). A mechanism arrow: squeezed through the glomerular membrane, then osmotic stress in the tubules. A criteria card: glomerular hematuria if ≥ 40% dysmorphic RBCs and/or ≥ 5% acanthocytes and/or ≥ 1 RBC cast per 50 low-power fields; cut-offs vary between studies (10–90%); phase contrast helps; automated analyzers can miss casts and dysmorphic RBCs. Isomorphic RBCs without casts → stones, tumors, infection, anticoagulation. Then two Maltese crosses side by side under polarized light: cholesterol (symmetrical arms) vs starch from gloves (asymmetrical arms).

cues.text: Red cells that come through a damaged glomerulus are squeezed through the filter, then stressed by changing salt concentrations in the tubules. They come out misshapen: dysmorphic.
The most characteristic is the acanthocyte, a ring-shaped cell with small blebs. Phase-contrast microscopy shows them best.
One proposed rule calls hematuria glomerular with at least 40 percent dysmorphic cells, or at least 5 percent acanthocytes, or a red-cell cast. Cut-offs vary between studies.
Round, uniform red cells without casts suggest bleeding lower down: stones, tumors, infection or excess anticoagulation. Automated analyzers can miss casts and dysmorphic cells.
One more look-alike. Under polarized light, cholesterol makes Maltese crosses with symmetrical arms. Glove starch makes crosses with asymmetrical arms: an artifact, not fat.

props.title: Isomorphic, no casts
lines: Analyzers can miss casts and dysmorphic RBCs

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “RBC casts are glomerular — full stop” (✓ usually, but they appear in some interstitial nephritis); “WBC casts mean pyelonephritis” (✓ also interstitial nephritis and nephritic syndrome); “A Maltese cross always means fat” (✓ glove starch makes asymmetrical crosses).

cues.text: Trap one: red-cell casts are glomerular, full stop. Usually, yes. But a biopsy study found them in nearly a third of interstitial nephritis cases.
Trap two: white-cell casts mean pyelonephritis. They can, but interstitial nephritis and nephritic syndrome produce them too.
Trap three: every Maltese cross is fat. No. Glove starch gives crosses with asymmetrical arms; cholesterol arms are symmetrical.

props.title: ✗ “RBC casts are glomerular — full stop.”
lines: ✓ Usually — but also some interstitial nephritis

scenes.title: The tubule keeps a souvenir
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The tubule keeps a souvenir.” Each cast is a souvenir of what was in the tubule: red cells → bleeding glomerulus; white cells → inflamed kidney; tubular cells → dying tubule; fat → leaking protein; wax → a tubule that stood still. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the tubule keeps a souvenir. Red cells mean a bleeding glomerulus, white cells an inflamed kidney, tubular cells a dying tubule, fat a protein leak, and wax a tubule that stood still.
Where it breaks: cast types overlap between diseases; isomorphic red cells can occur in glomerulonephritis; dysmorphic cut-offs vary; and analyzers miss casts, so the microscope still matters.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Isomorphic RBCs occur in GN too · cut-offs vary
Analyzers miss casts — use the microscope

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Cast = from the kidney · RBC casts + dysmorphic RBCs/acanthocytes → glomerular bleeding”, “WBC: AIN/nephritic/pyelo · RTE/granular: ATN · waxy: renal failure · fatty/OFB: nephrotic · starch cross is asymmetrical”.

cues.text: A cast proves the material came from the kidney, and its contents point to the disease — red-cell casts and dysmorphic red cells to glomerular bleeding, fat to nephrotic syndrome — while glove starch only imitates fat.

props.label: Cast = from the kidney · RBC casts + dysmorphic RBCs/acanthocytes → glomerular bleeding
WBC: AIN/nephritic/pyelo · RTE: ATN · waxy: renal failure · fat: nephrotic · starch ≠ fat

explanation.what: Plain language: casts are tiny protein plugs shaped in the kidney tubules; what gets stuck in them shows what is happening in the kidney. Scientific terms: uromodulin (Tamm–Horsfall protein), hyaline, granular, waxy, fatty, RBC, WBC, renal tubular epithelial (RTE), bacterial and pigment casts; oval fat bodies; dysmorphic RBCs, acanthocytes (G1 cells); polarized light microscopy.
explanation.why: Cells in the tubular lumen are trapped in uromodulin gel. Red cells reach the tubule mainly through a damaged glomerulus, where mechanical and osmotic stress makes them dysmorphic. In nephrotic syndrome, filtered lipoproteins are taken up by tubular cells (oval fat bodies). Cholesterol esters are birefringent and form symmetrical Maltese crosses.
explanation.measure: Examine at least 10 (optimally 20) fields at 100× and 400×; phase contrast helps dysmorphic RBCs. One proposed rule for glomerular hematuria: ≥ 40% dysmorphic RBCs and/or ≥ 5% acanthocytes and/or ≥ 1 RBC cast per 50 LPF (cut-offs in the literature range from 10% to 90%).
explanation.differs: Glomerular (dysmorphic RBCs, acanthocytes, RBC casts) vs non-glomerular hematuria (isomorphic RBCs: stones, urologic cancer, infection, anticoagulation); cholesterol (symmetrical) vs starch (asymmetrical) Maltese crosses.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: RBC casts and acanthocytes → nephritic/glomerular; fatty casts and oval fat bodies → nephrotic; RTE/granular → ATN; WBC casts → interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis; waxy → renal failure; starch artifact under polarized light.

comparisons.title: Maltese cross: cholesterol vs starch
comparisons.distinguisher: Arm symmetry under polarized light, plus context.

mnemonic.explanation: Each cast preserves what was in the tubule: red cells (bleeding glomerulus), white cells (inflamed kidney), tubular cells (dying tubule), fat (protein leak), wax (stagnant tubule).
mnemonic.limitation: Cast types overlap between diseases; isomorphic RBCs occur in glomerulonephritis; dysmorphic cut-offs vary; analyzers can miss casts.

analogyLimitations: The tubule, gel and cells are schematic tokens, not real sediment images.
Crystals, dipstick chemistry and specimen handling are covered in other lessons.
takeaway: A cast proves the material came from the kidney, and its contents point to the disease — red-cell casts and dysmorphic red cells to glomerular bleeding, fat to nephrotic syndrome — while glove starch only imitates fat.

questions.stem: Urine sediment shows RBC casts and 8% acanthocytes among the red cells. Where is the bleeding most likely coming from?

options.rationale: Correct. RBC casts and acanthocytes are markers of glomerular hematuria.
Incorrect. Casts form only in tubules, so the red cells passed through the kidney.
Incorrect. Stones typically give isomorphic RBCs without casts.
Incorrect. Contamination does not produce casts.

questions.stem: A patient with heavy proteinuria has round tubular cells packed with droplets that show symmetrical Maltese crosses under polarized light. What are they?

options.text: Oval fat bodies, consistent with nephrotic-range proteinuria
options.rationale: Correct. Lipid-laden tubular cells with cholesterol Maltese crosses are oval fat bodies.
Incorrect. Starch crosses have asymmetrical arms and are not inside tubular cells.
Incorrect. Oxalate crystals are envelope- or dumbbell-shaped, not lipid droplets in cells.
Incorrect. Yeast are not lipid-filled tubular cells.

questions.stem: A patient with acute kidney injury after a drug reaction has WBC casts, RTE cells and sterile pyuria. Which statement is correct?

options.text: WBC casts are not specific for pyelonephritis; interstitial nephritis also produces them
options.rationale: Correct. WBC casts occur in interstitial nephritis, nephritic syndrome and pyelonephritis.
Incorrect. Sterile pyuria and a drug trigger point to interstitial nephritis; bacterial casts would suggest pyelonephritis.

options.text: Casts here must come from the bladder
options.rationale: Incorrect. Casts form only in renal tubules.

options.text: Waxy casts would be expected first
options.rationale: Incorrect. Waxy casts reflect stagnant tubules in renal failure, not the inflammatory signature.

claims.text: Casts form in tubules from uromodulin (Tamm–Horsfall) trapping luminal contents; hyaline casts rise with exercise, dehydration, fever; read ≥ 10 fields at 100× and 400×.

RBC casts nephritic (rarely AIN); WBC casts AIN, nephritic, pyelonephritis; RTE/granular ATN; waxy renal failure acute or chronic; fatty casts and OFB nephrotic; bacterial casts pyelonephritis; pigment casts.

Dysmorphic RBCs and acanthocytes indicate glomerular bleeding; proposed criteria ≥ 40% / ≥ 5% / ≥ 1 RBC cast per 50 LPF; cut-offs vary; isomorphic RBCs in non-glomerular bleeding; analyzers miss casts.
Cholesterol Maltese crosses symmetrical; starch crosses asymmetrical.
Glitter cells point to pyelonephritis; > 30 WBC/hpf suggests acute UTI; scant mucus is normal; broad casts form in dilated tubules.
claims.note: Not taught; not in the sources read.

claims.text: Tubule, gel and cell tokens are schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 1 calls RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs “glomerular disease, full stop”; RBC casts were found in 29% of biopsy-proven acute interstitial nephritis (Gaggar 2024, citing Fogazzi). The lesson teaches “usually glomerular”.

Hit 5 assigns WBC casts to pyelonephritis and waxy casts to end-stage disease; Gaggar 2024 lists WBC casts in interstitial nephritis and nephritic syndrome as well, and waxy casts in acute as well as chronic renal failure.

morphology.note: Casts, cells and Maltese crosses are schematic tokens, not real sediment images.
